newsitem.title: USA: U.S. watches Zaire and issues travel warning.
newsitem.headline: U.S. watches Zaire and issues travel warning.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Friday U.S. officials were monitoring the rebellion in Zaire day-by-day, even hour-by-hour, to assess whether to evacuate U.S. citizens.

Asked if he believed evacuation would be needed, he said "that depends on a day-by-day assessment, it could be an hour-by-hour assessment, that we are following very closely and as usual we will take every measure possible to make sure our citizens are safe."

Also on Friday, the State Department announced a new warning to U.S. citizens to defer travel to Zaire and strongly encouraged dependents of U.S. Embassy personnel in Kinshasa to depart. The warning was issued "due to the uncertain political and security situation and the potential for unrest throughout the country," the department said.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said some 30 U.S. military planners were in the region, in Brazzaville and Libreville, in order to prepare contingency plans, and more were expected to arrive "in the next day or two."

Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said on Thursday the U.S. military was making contingency preparations to evacuate Americans from Zaire if necessary. France sent troops and planes to nearby Gabon and Congo in case evacuations weree needed.
Rebels who have been fighting since October 1996 to topple Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko seized the key city of Kisangani over the weekend.

Mobutu left France where he had undergone cancer treatment on Friday and returned home in an effort to salvage control of the Central African country. But Laurent Kabila's rebels rejected a call for a ceasefire followed by peace negotiations. "We negotiate first," Kabila said on arrival in Kisangani.
